claims.statement_en: Lebanon's health ministry gave a first toll for the Sep 17 pager blasts of 8-9 dead and roughly 2,750-2,800 wounded (about 200 critically).
claims.first_public: Sep 17 evening (Beirut), Lebanese health minister Firas Abiad: 8 dead, ~2,750 wounded, ~200 critical; later to Al Jazeera 9 dead incl. an 8-year-old girl

claims.statement_en: The pager-wave death toll was revised up to 12, including two children (Abiad, Sep 18), with about 2,800 wounded; on Sep 19 Abiad put pager-wave wounded at 2,323.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Abiad press conference: 12 dead incl. 2 children, 2,750-2,800 wounded, ~300 critical, 460 surgeries (mostly eyes)

claims.statement_en: The Sep 18 walkie-talkie blasts killed at least 14-20 people and wounded about 450 (health ministry figures on Sep 18).
claims.first_public: Sep 18 evening, Lebanese health ministry: 14 dead / ~450 wounded, raised to 20 / 450 that night

claims.statement_en: The walkie-talkie toll was later raised to 25 dead and 608 wounded (Abiad, Sep 19) and then 27 dead (Sep 21).
claims.first_public: Sep 19 ~12:00 UTC, Abiad press conference (25/608); Sep 21 update (27)

claims.statement_en: Together the two waves killed roughly 32-39 people (32 by Sep 19; 37 by Sep 20; 12 + 27 = 39 by Sep 21) and wounded about 3,000 or more.
claims.first_public: Sep 19, health ministry (32 over two days); 37 by Sep 19-20 (Abiad to NPR Sep 20: '37 and almost 3,000'); 12 + 27 = 39 by Sep 21; ministry total later 39 dead / 2,931 wounded

claims.statement_en: Israeli assessments held that Lebanon's official toll understated the real number of dead, with 'many dozens' or more killed.
claims.first_public: Sep 19, Ynet citing Israeli assessments

claims.statement_en: About 1,500 Hezbollah fighters were put out of action by the attacks, many of them blinded or having lost hands (Reuters, Sep 25, citing sources).
claims.first_public: Sep 25, Reuters citing a Hezbollah source (carried by Times of Israel; Reuters URL not located)

claims.statement_en: Most injuries were to the hands, eyes/face and abdomen, with many amputations and eye injuries.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 evening, Lebanese health minister Abiad and hospital staff

claims.statement_en: More than 500 people suffered eye injuries in the pager blasts, about 300 of whom lost their sight completely.
claims.first_public: Sep 19, MTV Lebanon 'MTV information'

claims.statement_en: Pagers also exploded in Syria, wounding Hezbollah members and others (14 wounded per the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights).
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~14:00-15:00 UTC, Syrian Observatory / Syrian and IRGC-linked media

claims.statement_en: 19 members of Iran's Revolutionary Guards were killed (and ~150 wounded) by pager explosions in Syria.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Saudi channel Al-Hadath citing sources

claims.statement_en: Children were among those killed (two children per Lebanon's health ministry).
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~15:30-16:30 UTC, Hezbollah statement (a girl killed) and Abiad (girl among 8 dead); two children per Abiad Sep 18

claims.statement_en: Fatima Abdullah, a girl of about 9-10, was killed in the Bekaa (Saraain) when her father's pager exploded at home.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 evening, AFP quoting relatives (unnamed girl, 10); named Fatima Abdallah of Saraain by AP (age 8) and at her Sep 18 funeral (family: 9; NYT, AP)

claims.statement_en: An 11-year-old boy, (Mohammad) Bilal Kanj, was killed by a pager blast; Hezbollah buried him as a scout.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Hezbollah funeral announcement / NYT and WaPo

claims.statement_en: The son of Hezbollah MP Ali Ammar (Mohammad Mahdi Ammar) was killed in the pager blasts.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 afternoon, Al-Hadath / An-Nahar sources; AP and AFP the same evening (AP later corrected the name to Mahdi Ammar)

claims.statement_en: The son of Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah was killed in the pager blasts.
claims.first_public: Sep 17, AFP first reported him killed, then corrected to 'alive but injured'

claims.statement_en: MP Hassan Fadlallah's son was injured (undergoing surgery), not killed; reports of his death were false.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 evening, AFP correction; LBCI 'death reports false'

claims.statement_en: Iran's ambassador to Lebanon, Mojtaba Amani, was wounded when a pager exploded.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~14:00 UTC, Iran's Mehr / IRNA, relayed by Reuters

claims.statement_en: Ambassador Amani lost one eye and his other eye was seriously injured.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, The New York Times citing IRGC members (relayed by Times of Israel Sep 18)

claims.statement_en: Ambassador Amani was only superficially / lightly injured and in good condition.
claims.first_public: Sep 17, IRNA / Mehr and the Iranian embassy on X

claims.statement_en: Health workers were among those killed (Abiad: two, later four, health-sector workers).
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Abiad via AFP (4 health workers among the 12 dead); HRW Sep 18 says two

claims.statement_en: Most of those wounded were civilians (Lebanese health minister Abiad, Sep 20).
claims.first_public: Sep 20, Abiad press statements

claims.statement_en: The killed and wounded were (overwhelmingly) Hezbollah members / fighters.
claims.first_public: Sep 17, Israeli and Arab media describing 'thousands of Hezbollah operatives wounded'

claims.statement_en: Most pager holders were not frontline fighters but administrative, logistic, social-service or rear-echelon Hezbollah members.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Lebanese analyst Nabih Awada on Al Jadeed; WaPo Sep 19 ('society in arms'); WaPo Oct 5 ('rear-echelon figures')

claims.statement_en: Senior Hezbollah commander Ibrahim Aqil had been wounded by a pager and was discharged from hospital on Sep 20, the day Israel killed him in Beirut.
claims.first_public: Sep 20, Haaretz / Israeli media

claims.statement_en: Hezbollah held Israel 'fully responsible' for the blasts.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~16:00 UTC, Hezbollah's second statement (its first statement said it was probing and did not blame Israel)

claims.statement_en: Lebanon's government (PM Mikati, Information Minister Makary, FM Bou Habib) blamed Israel and called the attack a violation of Lebanese sovereignty.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 evening, PM Najib Mikati ('criminal Israeli aggression'; asked the UN to stop Israel's 'technological war') and Information Minister Ziad Makary

claims.statement_en: Israel's Mossad planted explosives in the pagers before they reached Hezbollah (supply-chain sabotage, not a hack).
claims.first_public: Sep 17 evening (US time), NYT citing American and other officials; Sep 18 Reuters citing a senior Lebanese security source

claims.statement_en: US officials said Israel was behind the attack.
claims.first_public: Sep 17-18, Axios / NBC / Fox citing US officials

claims.statement_en: Israel did not claim responsibility and its military/government declined to comment on the blasts.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~13:30 UTC onward, IDF / PMO 'no comment'

claims.statement_en: Israeli President Isaac Herzog denied Israeli involvement ('I reject out of hand any connection'), saying Hezbollah had many enemies.
claims.first_public: Sep 22, Herzog to Sky News: 'I reject out of hand any connection'

claims.statement_en: Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi posted a Bible verse (Nahum 2:11, 'empty, void and waste, the heart melts...') read as hinting at Israeli responsibility.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Karhi on X (reported by Ynet Sep 18)

claims.statement_en: Netanyahu and senior ministers/security chiefs approved the operation at a meeting days before (Axios citing officials), without informing the Biden administration in advance.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 evening, Axios (Barak Ravid) citing US/Israeli officials

claims.statement_en: Netanyahu publicly confirmed (Nov 10, 2024) that he approved the pager operation, over objections from senior officials.
claims.first_public: Nov 10 2024, Netanyahu at the cabinet meeting, via spokesman Omer Dostri to AFP

claims.statement_en: The United States said it was not involved in and not aware in advance of the attacks (State Dept's Matthew Miller, Blinken, Kirby, Pentagon).
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~19:00 UTC, State Department spokesman Matthew Miller briefing

claims.statement_en: Taiwan's Gold Apollo said the AR-924 pagers carried its brand but were made and sold by its licensee BAC Consulting in Budapest.
claims.first_public: Sep 18 ~02:00-04:00 UTC, Gold Apollo statement / founder Hsu Ching-kuang to reporters

claims.statement_en: Hungary's government said BAC was a trading intermediary with no manufacturing or operational site in Hungary and the devices were never in Hungary.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Hungarian government spokesman Zoltán Kovács ('never in Hungary')

claims.statement_en: A Bulgaria-registered firm, Norta Global, owned by Norwegian citizen Rinson Jose, was linked to the pager deal (about EUR 1.6 million reportedly passed through Bulgaria to Hungary).
claims.first_public: Sep 19, Hungarian outlet Telex; Bulgarian probe announced Sep 19; Norway issued an international search request for Rinson Jose Sep 26

claims.statement_en: Bulgaria's State Agency for National Security said no pagers used in the Lebanon attack were imported, exported or manufactured in Bulgaria.
claims.first_public: ~Sep 20, Bulgarian State Agency for National Security (DANS)

claims.statement_en: The devices in the second wave were Icom IC-V82 walkie-talkies.
claims.first_public: Sep 18 ~15:00 UTC, photos / Al Jazeera, confirmed by Lebanon's telecom ministry

claims.statement_en: At ~15:30 the pagers received a (coded) message, appearing to come from Hezbollah's leadership, that triggered the explosives; the devices beeped before exploding.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~22:00 UTC, NYT citing officials; Sep 18 Reuters ('coded message')

claims.statement_en: Each pager held only a small charge of explosive, up to about 3 grams (Reuters source); later reporting described a ~6 g PETN sheet inside the battery.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Reuters citing a security source; Oct 16 Reuters (6 g)

claims.statement_en: The explosive was PETN, built into or attached to the device batteries (pagers and walkie-talkies).
claims.first_public: Sep 17 evening, Sky News Arabia sources (PETN on batteries); Sep 20 Reuters Lebanese source (walkie-talkie batteries laced with PETN)

claims.statement_en: BAC was an Israeli front: at least three shell companies were set up to hide that Israeli intelligence officers were producing the pagers (NYT, Sep 18).
claims.first_public: Sep 18, NYT citing three intelligence officers

claims.statement_en: Israel was involved in making the pagers and had planned the supply-chain operation for about 15 years (ABC News, citing a US intelligence source).
claims.first_public: Sep 19, ABC News (Josh Margolin) citing a US intelligence source

claims.statement_en: Hezbollah scanned and tested the pagers (including with airport scanners) without finding explosives, and was still handing them out hours before the blasts.
claims.first_public: Sep 20, Reuters exclusive (Laila Bassam, Maya Gebeily) citing two security sources

claims.statement_en: The pagers were designed so that reading the encrypted message required pressing two buttons, so users would likely hold them with both hands when they exploded (WaPo, Oct 5).
claims.first_public: Oct 5, The Washington Post citing Israeli, Arab and US officials

claims.statement_en: The pagers were designed and assembled in Israel under Mossad supervision (pitched to Hezbollah via a saleswoman in 2023); booby-trapped walkie-talkies had been introduced into Lebanon since 2015 (WaPo, Oct 5).
claims.first_public: Oct 5, The Washington Post

claims.statement_en: The pagers exploded because their lithium batteries overheated (e.g., from a cyberattack or overload).
claims.first_public: Sep 17, first AP version (archived 14:23 UTC) quoting a Hezbollah official that lithium batteries 'apparently exploded' after heating up; LBCI 'preliminary information'; WSJ (malware-induced overheating)

claims.statement_en: Israel set off the devices by hacking them or Hezbollah's network remotely (cyberattack, malware, high-frequency signals), without planted explosives.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~13:00-14:00 UTC, Hezbollah source to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed ('Israel hacked remotely'); MTV security sources Sep 18 (high-frequency waves)

claims.statement_en: The exploded pagers were issued to senior/high-ranking Hezbollah members.
claims.first_public: Sep 17, Axios source ('used widely, including by senior officials'); Welt video expert Shlomo Shpiro ('only distributed to high-ranking members')

claims.statement_en: Israel detonated the pagers earlier than planned because Hezbollah members (two operatives) had grown suspicious; they had been meant as the opening blow of an all-out war.
claims.first_public: Sep 17-18, Al-Monitor exclusive (two Hezbollah members suspicious); Sep 18 Axios citing three US officials ('use it or lose it') and a former Israeli official (opening blow of all-out war)

claims.statement_en: Israeli sources said the strategic aim was deterrence: about 4,000 'targeted' hits, wounding rather than killing, and 'not the last move'.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Ynet citing people familiar with the operation

claims.statement_en: UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the simultaneous targeting of thousands of people without knowing who held the devices violated international human rights law and international humanitarian law, and demanded an independent investigation and accountability.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, OHCHR comment (independent investigation, accountability); Sep 20 to the UN Security Council (violates IHRL and, where applicable, IHL)

claims.statement_en: International humanitarian law prohibits booby-traps in the form of apparently harmless portable objects (argument applied to the pagers by Türk and legal experts, e.g., CCW Amended Protocol II).
claims.first_public: Sep 18, legal commentators (HRW, academics); Sep 20 Türk at the UN Security Council

claims.statement_en: EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the attacks: even if targeted, they caused 'heavy, indiscriminate collateral damage among civilians, including children'.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Borrell statement on behalf of the EU

claims.statement_en: Ireland's Tánaiste and Foreign Minister Micheál Martin condemned the attack as showing reckless disregard for human life and as a breach of international humanitarian law / the Geneva Conventions.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Micheál Martin to reporters in Dublin (per RND/PA and Al-Manar in the corpus); external report of 'wanton disregard' and 'yes, absolutely' on a Geneva breach ~Sep 24

claims.statement_en: Spain's foreign ministry said the device attacks violated international humanitarian law.
claims.first_public: Sep 19, Spanish MFA communiqué 051

claims.statement_en: Russia strongly condemned the attack (MFA: 'thousands of innocent people' hurt, a blatant violation of Lebanese sovereignty, requires an international investigation; Kremlin: risks escalation in an explosive region).
claims.first_public: Sep 18, MFA spokeswoman Maria Zakharova and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov ('possible trigger')

claims.statement_en: Iran condemned the blasts as 'mass murder' / a 'terrorist act' by Israel and reserved the right to respond to the injury of its ambassador.
claims.first_public: Sep 17-18, Iranian FM spokesman Nasser Kanaani, FM Araghchi, President Pezeshkian

claims.statement_en: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said the attack 'clearly and unequivocally violates international humanitarian law' and demanded to know whether US assistance was involved.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Ocasio-Cortez on X

claims.statement_en: Former CIA director and defense secretary Leon Panetta said in a CBS News interview (CBS News Sunday Morning) that the attack was 'a form of terrorism'.
claims.first_public: Sep 22, CBS News Sunday Morning interview

claims.statement_en: Lebanon's health minister Firas Abiad called the attacks a war crime because most of the wounded were civilians.
claims.first_public: Sep 20, Abiad press statements

claims.statement_en: Lebanon's health minister Firas Abiad called it 'an indiscriminate attack where a lot of civilians were involved'.
claims.first_public: Sep 19-20, Abiad in international media interviews (web-research pass; NPR transcript among its sources)

claims.statement_en: Lebanese government officials called the attack terrorism: FM Abdallah Bou Habib at the UN Security Council (Sep 20) and Labour Minister Mustafa Bayram ('a terrorist crime').
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Labour Minister Mustafa Bayram; Sep 20, FM Abdallah Bou Habib at the UN Security Council ('Isn't this terrorism?')

claims.statement_en: The operation was a precise, discriminate strike on Hezbollah operatives (lawful targeting of combatants), not an indiscriminate attack.
claims.first_public: Sep 17-18, Israeli sources and Western commentators/experts

claims.statement_en: Defense Minister Yoav Gallant said Israel was at 'the start of a new phase in the war', with the centre of gravity moving north.
claims.first_public: Sep 18 evening, Gallant at Ramat David air base

claims.statement_en: Hezbollah vowed that Israel would receive its 'just punishment' for the attack.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~16:00-17:00 UTC, Hezbollah statement; repeated by Nasrallah Sep 19

claims.statement_en: A Hezbollah official told Reuters the blasts were the group's 'biggest security breach' (in nearly a year of war).
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~13:30-14:00 UTC, Reuters citing an anonymous Hezbollah official

claims.statement_en: Nasrallah said the attacks could be considered a declaration of war.
claims.first_public: Sep 19 ~14:00 UTC, Nasrallah televised speech

claims.statement_en: Nasrallah acknowledged Hezbollah had suffered a severe, unprecedented blow.
claims.first_public: Sep 19 ~14:00 UTC, Nasrallah speech

claims.statement_en: Nasrallah said Israel intended to kill at least 4,000 people in one minute (5,000 over the two days), but many pagers were switched off or not yet distributed.
claims.first_public: Sep 19 ~14:00 UTC, Nasrallah speech

claims.statement_en: Nasrallah said Hezbollah's senior leaders did not carry the type of pagers that exploded.
claims.first_public: Sep 19 ~14:00 UTC, Nasrallah speech

claims.statement_en: Hezbollah fired Fadi-1/Fadi-2 rockets at Rafael defence-industry facilities north of Haifa as an 'initial response' to the 'pager and wireless massacre'.
claims.first_public: Sep 22 early morning, Hezbollah statement

claims.statement_en: Lebanese hospitals were overwhelmed by the influx of wounded.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~13:00-14:00 UTC, health ministry alerts, AP photographers, hospital staff

claims.statement_en: Authorities and airlines banned pagers and walkie-talkies on flights (Lebanon's civil aviation authority for Beirut flights from Sep 19; Emirates from Oct 4).
claims.first_public: Sep 19, Lebanese Directorate General of Civil Aviation circular 30/2

claims.statement_en: The Lebanese army carried out controlled detonations of suspicious pagers and radios found across Beirut and elsewhere.
claims.first_public: Sep 18, Lebanese army / NNA

claims.statement_en: Hezbollah used pagers because, unlike mobile phones, they are hard or impossible to locate or track (receive-only, not logged into a network).
claims.first_public: Sep 17, explainers (Reuters background; German public broadcasters)

claims.statement_en: Hezbollah turned to pagers after Nasrallah told members in February 2024 to stop using (or bury) their mobile phones.
claims.first_public: Sep 17, background in AP/CNN/Reuters explainers (speech of Feb 13, 2024)

claims.statement_en: Ordinary smartphones cannot be made to explode by a remote hack alone; the attack required explosives physically planted in the devices.
claims.first_public: Sep 17-18, tech explainers (CNN, t-online, Bild, MTV)

claims.statement_en: Lebanese authorities urged people to stay away from or throw away pagers and wireless devices after the blasts.
claims.first_public: Sep 17 ~13:00-14:00 UTC, Lebanese health ministry statement
